about: #283 / ADR-0014 decision 6, spec #279 — the hand-labeled measurement grid the INDUSTRY labeler must pass before it is trusted, and the permanent regression harness for every later prompt or vocabulary change. Drafted by the agent 2026-08-23; ALL 12 flagged entries owner-arbitrated the same day (arbitration:true, rulings in the notes) — 11 drafts ratified, near-07 overruled and the public-and-social group split (vocabulary v2). Real model calls AND real employer web lookups (both evidence sources, as production wires them): run it deliberately (pnpm --filter @jobcrush/api eval:industry-labeler, with ANTHROPIC_API_KEY set), never in fast-lane CI. The `pairs` section is pure data against the published group tree — it costs nothing and is the check that catches a group drawn too wide.

expectations.confirmed: expectedIndustries must match as a SET — a placement into the wrong industry, or one that names a spurious second industry, is a miss, not partial credit.
expectations.unmapped: the honest no-industry answer, for employers no published industry covers. A near-miss business landing here is the labeler working, not failing.
expectations.expectedConfidence: a map of industryId to ordinal, asserted only where the right ordinal is not in doubt and only for the industries named — REPORTED as its own rate, never barred: the industries are the gate.
expectations.multi-industry: the employer's own industry plus the industry the work was SERVED into, both true of one job (spec #279). The second industry must come from the person's own lines showing substantial, repeated work in it — one client mentioned once (ctrl-*) is not a second industry, and neither is a sales page listing sectors served.
expectations.lookup: every case's employer is looked up live through makeEmployerLookup at run time, cached in-run — the same wiring production runs. A fictional employer's lookup honestly finding nothing IS the unknown-small-employer condition (unk-*).
expectations.pairs: closeness read off the published group tree, no model call. near must read near (transferable credit at x0.9), far must read far (no credit). A far pair reading near means the group is drawn too wide: split it, re-publish the vocabulary, re-run — that gate is this section's whole reason to exist.

cases.note: OWNER ARBITRATED 2026-08-23: it-services alone. An employer gets ONE stamp — its MAIN business — even when its self-description uses two of our words (Infosys genuinely has a consulting arm; it is a small slice of an IT-delivery company). A second industry comes only from the person's own lines serving a client industry, never from the employer's description — otherwise every employee of every hybrid company would collect credit on both. A CV naming 'Infosys Consulting' as the employer is a different job judged on its own evidence.

OWNER ARBITRATED 2026-08-23: near — ruled at the COMPANY level, deliberately: both sell people's expertise into client companies. The person-level difference (a consultant's work is nothing like a recruiter's) is the family axis's fact and stays guarded by family bars, so this dial only transfers the business world at x0.9.

OWNER ARBITRATED 2026-08-23: FAR — overruling the draft (near). Care and teaching are different businesses that merely share a non-profit purpose, so the public-and-social group was split (vocabulary v2: health-and-care, education-and-training) and a hospital career credits a school bar nothing. Keeps its near- id on purpose, family precedent str-13: the history of a case that MOVED is worth more than a tidy number.
load-bearing for the consultant cases: consulting years are NOT bank years — only the second industry on the job carries bank credit
the 'IT in banks' trap: an IT-services career is not finance experience; the served industry, when the lines show it, is the honest route to that credit
the health-insurer boundary from both scope sentences: paying for care and delivering it stay far apart
the edtech boundary: teaching and selling learning software stay far apart
retailers run warehouses; the industries still read far — warehousing sold as a service is the logistics scope, a retailer's own shed is not
the manufacturing scope's own edge: making goods and selling them to the public are two businesses
airlines move the passengers, hotels host them — the hospitality scope says so itself
